August 4, 2026




 Paramount CEO says politics fueling Warner Bros 







WASHINGTON, United States (AFP)—Paramount CEO David Ellison said Tuesday that the legal battle over his proposed multibillion-dollar takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery was fueled by politics rather than concerns over market share.

His remarks in an opinion piece published in The New York Times came as a federal judge set a March 2027 trial date for the antitrust challenges to the megamerger.

Ellison’s Paramount Skydance agreed late last month to delay its $110 billion merger with Warner Bros. to June 2027 while the US lawsuit seeking to block the deal moves forward.

If the merger eventually closes, the new combined company would reshape the entertainment and media industry, in addition to delivering a major win to its owners, the Ellison family, who are close allies of US President Donald Trump.

If the deal doesn’t close, the Ellison family could be on the hook for billions in kill fees.

In a combative op-ed, Ellison argued that the fight over the deal “is not really about market share.”

“The issue is whether I can be trusted as a steward of Warner’s CNN. There has been speculation about my politics, my loyalties, my intentions,” he wrote.

In their complaint against the deal, 12 Democratic-led US states claim the combined company would control roughly 27 percent of wide-release theatrical film distribution and a similar percentage of basic cable channel licensing.

“We are eager to continue to make our case in court… to ensure this unlawful merger never sees the light of day,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in a statement last month.

The deal would include CNN, one of the largest US cable news networks and a frequent target of Trump’s insults and attacks over coverage critical of his administration.

On June 12 the Trump administration approved the blockbuster deal without demanding a single change, clearing the way for one of the largest media mergers in years.

Ellison argued that he held views across the political spectrum, “just like most Americans.”

“When it comes to our news operations, I do not aspire to lead these companies to bend their newsrooms to my views,” he said. “I believe that news should be based on facts and truth.”

Ellison’s Skydance acquired CBS News in mid-2025, with the major US broadcaster reaching a $16 million settlement with Trump over coverage of presidential candidate Kamala Harris in the same period.

Shortly after CBS became a part of Paramount Skydance, the company brought in Bari Weiss — a longstanding critic of progressive politics — to lead its news division.

Many CBS News journalists quit following Weiss’s appointment, alleging curbs on their editorial independence.

David Ellison is the son of Oracle founder Larry Ellison, who Forbes says has a net worth of more than $185 billion, making him the seventh richest person in the world.

news.title: Armed man arrested near Trump's golf course days before scheduled presidential visit
news.text: A 38-year-old California man was arrested on Sunday near US President Donald Trump's golf club in Rancho Palos Verdes, Los Angeles, shortly before the president arrived for a scheduled visit.The man drew the attention of plainclothes FBI agents operating in the area, according to authorities. Agents found a loaded handgun and a magazine containing ammunition inside his vehicle.A subsequent search of his home uncovered numerous firearms, ammunition, protective vests, and notebooks containing material that authorities described as concerning. Officials said no concrete threat had been identified, though the investigation remains ongoing.Initial findings showed that authorities seized an improperly modified AR rifle, a .45 caliber 1911 handgun, two radios, a protective vest, and high-capacity magazines.During a search of the suspect, investigators also found a magazine containing 16 hollow-point rounds. The handgun discovered in his vehicle was loaded, with a round already in the chamber.Trump attends fundraising event at the golf clubThe suspect had already been under investigation by El Segundo police on suspicion of robbery. He was also arrested on suspicion of carrying a concealed weapon and possessing prohibited ammunition.Investigators from the FBI's Joint Terrorism Task Force searched his home in Downey on Monday. The case was later transferred to the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office for review, and additional charges are expected to be filed.Trump had been scheduled to attend a Republican National Committee dinner at his golf course Tuesday evening.Gunshots heard at annual White House dinner earlier this yearAbout four months earlier, gunshots were heard during the annual White House Correspondents' Dinner, prompting Secret Service agents to remove Trump, first lady Melania Trump, and Vice President JD Vance from the stage.The incident began before the entertainment program started, when a man carrying several weapons charged toward security checkpoints in the hotel lobby from about 50 meters away.A confrontation followed, during which shots were fired and a Secret Service agent was shot at close range.Security personnel quickly evacuated Trump, the vice president, and other senior officials from the head table to a secure area. A rapid response team then subdued the suspect and removed him from the premises.

news.title: Trump-backed John James wins Michigan’s GOP primary for governor
news.text: Rep. John James has won Michigan’s Republican nomination for governor, NBC News projects. James, who represents the Detroit suburbs, prevailed in the primary despite being vastly outspent by his opponent, wealthy businessman Perry Johnson. President Donald Trump, despite harboring early concerns that a bid for higher office would put the two-term congressman’s competitive House district at risk, endorsed James and last week traveled to the state to campaign for him. James, 45, will face Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, the winner of Tuesday’s Democratic primary, this fall in one of the most fiercely contested battleground states. Term limits prevent Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat, from seeking re-election. An Army veteran who lost two Senate races before winning his House seat in 2022, James presented himself throughout the race as a capable public servant with applicable business experience, given his work with his family’s logistics company. “This is an amazing state with all the great ingredients, but for the past seven-and-a-half years, under Gretchen Whitmer, we’ve been led to higher taxes, more crime on the roads — and frankly, the roads we have aren’t fixed yet,” James said during a televised debate last month, throwing back to Whitmer’s 2018 campaign vow to “fix the damn roads.” “We’re going to work together to make sure that our children can read, to make sure that we put criminals in jail, and we hold those accountable who continue to let them back out,” James added. “And we’re going to be making sure that we come together to accomplish the mission of increasing hope and purpose with tested, positive leadership that has actually been tested from the battlefield to business to delivering for you right now.” Johnson, 78, pounded the state with more than $31 million worth of ads, according to AdImpact, an ad-tracking firm. He drew on his work in quality control and improving business efficiencies while campaigning on a plan to eliminate the state’s income tax. Johnson also drew on his personal wealth, self-funding his run while declining political donations. “In the state of Michigan, people are really tired of the politicians,” Johnson told NBC News in an interview last month. “I am an outsider. Nobody denies this fact. I’m the outsider of outsiders.” James’ campaign spent a fraction on advertising — $2.8 million, according to AdImpact. One potential factor in the results was the absence of former state Attorney General Mike Cox, who dropped out of the primary on July 17 and threw his support to James. Several polls had shown Cox grabbing a substantial share of the Republican vote and raised the possibility of an unpredictable three-way split that could have benefited Johnson. Meanwhile, the general election challenge eased a bit for Democrats in May when former Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan ended his independent bid for governor. Duggan, a longtime Democrat, had expressed disappointment with both major political parties but caught attention — and grief — from Democrats who noted his reluctance to aggressively criticize Trump. Michigan voters have not elected a Democrat to succeed a Democrat as governor in more than 65 years. Benson deputy campaign manager Alyssa Bradley wrote in an email that the secretary of state “begins the general election with something no other candidate can claim: a record of delivering.” An accompanying campaign memo took a parting shot at both Republican candidates for governor. “John James and Perry Johnson spent this year lobbing personal attacks at each other and competing for Donald Trump’s attention, not talking to Michigan families about the cost of housing, healthcare, or keeping the lights on,” the memo read. “Both Republican candidates focused on election denying and Donald Trump, while Jocelyn has stayed focused on the issues affecting Michigan families every day.”

news.title: How are drones changing Ukraine's battlefield strategy?
news.text:
Although the figures have not been independently verified, the statement reflects Ukraine's growing reliance on drones to compensate for manpower and equipment limitations while targeting Russian forces across the front line.
As negotiations remain stalled and both sides continue investing heavily in drone technology, unmanned systems have evolved from a supporting capability into one of the defining features of modern warfare. The latest claims also highlight how military success is increasingly measured not only by territorial gains but by technological innovation and sustained battlefield adaptation.
What did Zelenskyy claim about Ukraine's drone campaign?
In his evening address, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that Ukrainian drone units had killed or seriously wounded 30,272 Russian soldiers during July.
According to Zelenskyy, the figures were based on military data supported by video evidence collected by Ukrainian forces. He also claimed that Russia was losing approximately 30,000 personnel each month during the conflict.
The Ukrainian president said the reported casualties specifically resulted from drone operations conducted by Ukrainian military units rather than from all forms of combat combined.
The figures have not been independently verified, and Russian authorities did not immediately comment on the claims. During armed conflicts, casualty estimates released by the parties involved frequently differ, and independent confirmation is often difficult because of restricted access to active combat zones.
Beyond discussing military operations, Zelenskyy also addressed ongoing diplomatic contacts involving the United States and other international partners. He said Ukraine remained in regular communication with representatives connected to US President Donald Trump's administration while preparations continued for possible future negotiations.
Although the reported casualty figures remain unverified, the announcement illustrates the importance Ukraine now places on demonstrating the effectiveness of its expanding drone capabilities.
The statement also reflects how battlefield assessments increasingly emphasize technological performance alongside conventional military operations.
Why have drones become so important in the war?
The conflict in Ukraine has transformed drones from relatively limited reconnaissance tools into some of the most influential weapons on the modern battlefield.
At the beginning of the war, unmanned aircraft were primarily used to observe enemy positions, direct artillery fire and collect intelligence. As the conflict evolved, both Ukraine and Russia rapidly expanded their use of drones capable of carrying explosives, attacking armored vehicles and striking targets located far behind front lines.
Several factors explain this transformation. Drones are generally less expensive than many conventional military systems while providing commanders with continuous battlefield awareness and precision strike capabilities.
Unmanned systems also reduce risks to military personnel because they can perform dangerous missions without placing pilots or soldiers directly in harm's way.
Technological improvements have further expanded drone capabilities. Modern systems increasingly incorporate artificial intelligence, autonomous navigation, secure communications and improved sensors that enhance operational effectiveness.
The war has also encouraged rapid innovation. Military units frequently modify commercially available drones or develop new designs capable of responding quickly to changing battlefield conditions.
As a result, drones have become essential tools for reconnaissance, surveillance, logistics support, electronic warfare and direct attacks against military targets.
The conflict is now widely regarded by military analysts as one of the first large-scale wars in which unmanned systems have become central rather than supplementary elements of military operations.
How do military drones influence modern combat?
Military drones affect warfare by changing how armed forces gather intelligence, engage targets and allocate military resources.
Reconnaissance drones provide commanders with continuous aerial surveillance, allowing military units to monitor enemy movements, identify equipment concentrations and assess battlefield conditions in real time.
Attack drones expand these capabilities by carrying explosive payloads capable of striking vehicles, artillery positions, logistics facilities or command centers. Some are designed for repeated missions, while others function as loitering munitions that destroy themselves after reaching their targets.
The availability of relatively inexpensive drones creates new tactical challenges. Expensive tanks, artillery systems and air defense equipment may become vulnerable to weapons costing only a small fraction of their value.
Drones also influence military decision-making by increasing transparency on the battlefield. Constant aerial observation makes concealment more difficult while enabling faster responses to changing situations.
Electronic warfare has therefore become increasingly important. Both sides employ technologies designed to jam communications, interfere with satellite navigation or disable enemy drones before they reach intended targets.
The growing importance of unmanned systems has encouraged militaries worldwide to reconsider traditional force structures, procurement priorities and training programs.
The experience gained in Ukraine is expected to influence military planning internationally for many years because it demonstrates how rapidly technological innovation can reshape conventional warfare.
Why are casualty figures difficult to verify during war?
Casualty statistics released during armed conflicts often become subjects of considerable uncertainty because independent verification is rarely possible.
Governments and military organizations typically publish figures based on their own intelligence, operational reports or battlefield assessments. However, opposing sides frequently release different estimates reflecting their respective information sources and strategic communications.
Independent organizations generally face substantial obstacles when attempting to verify military casualties. Active combat zones may remain inaccessible, official records may be unavailable and battlefield conditions often prevent comprehensive investigations.
Military casualties also involve different categories, including those killed, wounded, missing or captured. Different governments may apply varying methodologies when reporting such figures, making direct comparisons difficult.
Technological evidence such as drone footage, satellite imagery and intercepted communications may support specific claims but often cannot independently confirm total casualty numbers across an entire front.
As a result, international observers frequently describe battlefield casualty figures as estimates unless independently verified by multiple reliable sources.
The Ukrainian president's statement regarding July drone operations therefore reflects Ukraine's official assessment, while independent confirmation remains unavailable at this stage.
Understanding these limitations helps explain why wartime casualty statistics should generally be interpreted cautiously until additional evidence becomes available.
What role do drones play alongside diplomacy?
Although military operations continue, Ukraine's leadership also remains engaged in diplomatic efforts aimed at finding a possible political solution to the conflict.
In his remarks, Zelenskyy said Ukraine continues maintaining regular contacts with representatives connected to the United States while expressing expectations regarding future diplomatic activity involving Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
He also noted cooperation with other international partners, particularly countries in the Gulf region, regarding security and diplomatic initiatives.
These comments illustrate that military operations and diplomatic negotiations often proceed simultaneously rather than sequentially. Governments frequently seek to strengthen their negotiating positions while continuing military activities.
The use of drones may therefore influence diplomacy indirectly by affecting battlefield conditions, military capabilities and perceptions of strategic balance.
Negotiations between Russia and Ukraine have experienced repeated interruptions since the conflict began. Although several rounds of talks have taken place under international mediation, substantial disagreements remain regarding conditions for a comprehensive settlement.
The continued expansion of drone warfare reflects the reality that military operations remain central while diplomatic channels continue facing significant obstacles.
Consequently, technological developments on the battlefield increasingly influence the broader political environment surrounding negotiations.
What does Ukraine's drone strategy reveal about the future of warfare?
Ukraine's expanding reliance on drones reflects broader transformations that are reshaping military doctrine worldwide.
Traditional military power has often emphasized large numbers of tanks, combat aircraft and heavily armed formations. The conflict demonstrates that relatively affordable unmanned systems can significantly influence battlefield outcomes when combined with effective intelligence and command structures.
Future armed forces are therefore expected to invest more heavily in artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, electronic warfare, secure communications and counter-drone technologies.
At the same time, drone warfare also creates new challenges. Cybersecurity, electronic interference and protection against autonomous attacks are becoming increasingly important components of national defense planning.
Countries observing the conflict are studying how rapidly commercial technologies can be adapted for military purposes and how innovation cycles have accelerated compared with traditional weapons procurement.
The conflict has also shown that technological superiority alone does not guarantee military success. Effective integration of drones with conventional forces, logistics, intelligence and command systems remains essential.
Regardless of the precise casualty figures reported by either side, one conclusion has become increasingly clear: unmanned systems are no longer secondary battlefield tools but central elements of contemporary military strategy.
The evolution of drone warfare in Ukraine is therefore likely to shape defense planning, military investment and operational doctrine around the world long after the conflict itself eventually ends.

news.title: Armed man arrested at Trump’s LA golf course ahead of president’s visit  - Antigua Tribune – Daily
news.text:
A man carrying a loaded handgun and hollow-point ammunition has been arrested at Donald Trump’s Los Angeles-area golf club, days before a scheduled visit by the US president, local authorities said.

The man, arrested on Sunday at the Trump National Golf Club in Rancho Palos Verdes, was identified by the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as 38-year-old Jeanine John Taele. The department said he had been seen photographing and filming the grounds while appearing to monitor security preparations ahead of Trump’s scheduled appearance at a Republican Party fundraising dinner on Tuesday.

Deputies said they found a 16-round magazine loaded with ammunition in his pocket, and later recovered a loaded pistol with a round chambered, along with a second loaded magazine, from his vehicle in the golf course car park.

Officials said Taele had already been under investigation by the El Segundo Police Department over a separate robbery case.

On Monday, detectives working with the FBI’s Joint Terrorism Task Force searched Taele’s Downey home, where they said they recovered an illegally modified rifle, a second pistol, body armour, high-capacity magazines, bulk ammunition and other radio signal devices and notebooks containing what officials described only as “concerning statements”.

The sheriff’s department said it had not identified any credible threat to the public and that Taele is being held without bail while prosecutors weigh charges.

Trump’s visit is part of a broader campaign swing through California and Nevada ahead of the November midterm elections.

news.title: Oil price today: Crude steadies below $80 as Hormuz blockade keeps investors on edge
news.text: Oil prices rose slightly on Wednesday after two days of steep losses, with markets closely watching efforts to end the US-Iran war and restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.Brent crude futures rose 31 cents, or 0.39%, to $79.67 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude gained 11 cents, or 0.15%, to $75.88 a barrel.The modest recovery comes after steep losses seen earlier in the week. Earlier on Tuesday, Qatar said that mediators were making progress in efforts to end the conflict. The comments pushed oil prices lower, although Tehran denied US President Donald Trump's claim that talks were already under way.Brent settled below $80 a barrel on Tuesday for the first time since July 13.“The main sticking point appears to be whether Iran will continue to insist on a degree of control over the waterway, and whether the US will stand its ground and refuse that outcome,” analysts from IG said in a note cited by Reuters.Brent had closed more than 5% lower on Tuesday, extending the sharp declines recorded on Monday amid hopes that an agreement could be reached soon. Before the war began, around 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas passed through the Strait of Hormuz. In March alone, oil prices had risen 50%.Qatar's Emiri office said US President Donald Trump and Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani discussed efforts to narrow differences between Washington and Tehran and improve the prospects for a lasting settlement during a phone call on Tuesday.Trump said on Monday that talks with Tehran had begun and described the situation as Iran's "last chance" to reach a deal. Iranian officials, however, maintained that no negotiations with the United States were taking place.Market participants were also awaiting official US inventory data later on Wednesday.According to market sources citing figures from the American Petroleum Institute, US crude and gasoline inventories increased last week, while distillate stocks declined.Crude inventories rose by about 2.7 million barrels in the week ended July 31, the sources said, speaking on condition of anonymity.Official inventory data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), the statistical arm of the US Department of Energy, is scheduled to be released at 10:30 am ET (1430 GMT) on Wednesday.Meanwhile, even as global crude benchmarks have continued to inch higher, the spike is far lower than the $126 per barrel levels seen earlier during the conflict.Get the latest Business News and Live updates. news.title: Oil prices steady after two-day decline amid optimism over US-Iran peace deal; Brent crude trades below $80 per barrel
news.text: US-Iran war: Oil prices remained under pressure after falling for two consecutive sessions, amid optimism that a deal could be reached to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restore the flow of crude supplies from the Persian Gulf.Brent crude traded below $80 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) hovered near $76 after plunging more than 10% over the previous two trading sessions.What's driving crude oil prices?Qatar announced on Tuesday that an interim proposal had been prepared, while both the United States and Iran indicated progress in negotiations aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz.Oil prices have fallen sharply over the past two weeks after US President Donald Trump said he had delayed fresh military strikes on Iran to allow more time for diplomatic talks. However, even if a temporary agreement is reached to restore commercial shipping through the strait, it may not bring a lasting end to the conflict or address Washington's concerns over Iran's nuclear programme.The previous ceasefire between the US and Iran lasted less than a month before breaking down over tensions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz. The renewed conflict triggered a nearly $32 swing in Brent crude prices last month as hostilities spread to the Red Sea. A later pause in fighting during late July, intended to support diplomatic efforts, also eventually collapsed.According to a Bloomberg report, Trump also spoke with Qatar's Emir, Sheikh Tamim Bin Hamad Al-Thani, on Tuesday to discuss efforts to ease tensions between Washington and Tehran, according to the Qatari government. The White House confirmed the call but did not disclose further details.In another sign of possible diplomatic progress, Iran is reportedly considering allowing European countries to clear mines from the Strait of Hormuz, according to diplomats familiar with the discussions. Separately, Iran's foreign ministry said talks with Oman had been constructive and focused on ensuring safe navigation through the strategic waterway, state-run IRIB News reported.Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia has held discussions with Yemen's Houthi rebels through Omani mediators in an effort to prevent the conflict from expanding, according to people familiar with the matter. Sources added that the kingdom is also preparing military contingency plans in case negotiations fail.On the supply side, US crude oil inventories increased by 2.7 million barrels last week, while stockpiles at Cushing, Oklahoma—the delivery hub for WTI crude—rose by 2.4 million barrels. If confirmed by official government data later on Wednesday, it would mark the largest weekly increase at Cushing since March and push inventories back above the 20 million-barrel level, which is widely viewed as the minimum required for smooth operations.(With inputs from Bloomberg)Disclaimer: This story is for educational purposes only. news.title: Man with gun in car arrested at Trump golf course before US president’s visit
news.text:
A man carrying ammunition and with a gun in his car was arrested on Sunday at US President Donald Trump’s Los Angeles-area golf course after appearing to monitor security preparations two days ahead of Trump’s fundraiser there, authorities said on Tuesday.
The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department said Jeanine John Taele, 38, was taking photos and video and had a 16-round magazine with ammunition in his pocket.
Authorities recovered a loaded pistol in his car. Law enforcement searched his home in the nearby city of Downey on Monday and found a plethora of firearms, magazines and ammunition, body armour and notebooks with “concerning statements”.
The sheriff’s department announced the arrest as Trump was preparing to arrive for the Republican National Committee dinner at the Trump National Golf Course in the suburb of Rancho Palos Verdes just south of Los Angeles. The department did not elaborate on what the notebooks’ “concerning statements” were or whether the man was planning an attack on the president or event.
Taele was charged with several felonies including second-degree robbery, receiving a large-capacity magazine and possession of a short-barrelled rifle or shotgun. He was also charged with carrying a concealed firearm in a vehicle, a misdemeanour.
He pleaded not guilty to all the charges Monday and was ordered to stay away from the golf course and not possess weapons. His bail was set at US$250,000.

It wasn’t clear if he had a lawyer, and family members could not immediately be reached for comment.
The sheriff’s department said when they made contact with Taele on Sunday, they had determined he was being investigated by the El Segundo Police Department for robbery.
The sheriff’s department said there is “no credible threat to our communities”.
Trump has been the target of multiple assassination attempts since launching his most recent presidential campaign.
In July 2024, Trump was targeted during a campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania. A gunman killed an audience member and lightly wounded the then-candidate in the ear.
A few months later, another armed man was arrested on a West Palm Beach golf course where Trump was playing a round.
In April, Trump was evacuated from a reception in Washington after an armed man attempted to enter the venue, triggering a shoot-out with security personnel.
Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

news.title: Scott Bessent draws on hedge fund instincts to help rescue yen
news.text: Scott Bessent wanted to help Japan prop up its currency. So he decided to let the media spy on his notepad, where a to-do list included buying as much as $10 billion in yen.It was an unorthodox tactic, but that’s become a Bessent hallmark. In a previous life on Wall Street, he made $1 billion on big currency bets while working for George Soros. As U.S. President Donald Trump’s Treasury secretary, he launched a high-risk rescue plan for Argentina. Now, he’s coming to the aid of another U.S. ally.The joint campaign by Washington and Tokyo to shore up the yen is the first of its kind in almost three decades. Beyond the notepad maneuver, Bessent has tapped a range of tools that surprised some Treasury watchers, like deploying U.S. holdings of euros and talking up a Federal Reserve facility that Japan could use.

news.title: Authorities say a man carrying ammo was monitoring security at Trump golf course near LA
news.text: LOS ANGELES — A man carrying ammunition and with a gun in his car was arrested Sunday at President Donald Trump’s Los Angeles-area golf course after appearing to monitor security preparations two days ahead of Trump’s fundraiser there, authorities said Tuesday.The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department said Jeanine John Taele, 38, was taking photos and video and had a 16-round magazine with ammunition in his pocket. Authorities recovered a loaded pistol in his car. Law enforcement searched his home in the nearby city of Downey on Monday and found a plethora of firearms, magazines and ammunition, body armor and notebooks with “concerning statements.”The sheriff’s department announced the arrest as Trump was preparing to arrive for the Republican National Committee dinner at the Trump National Golf Course in the suburb of Rancho Palos Verdes just south of Los Angeles. The department did not elaborate on what the notebooks' “concerning statements” were or whether the man was planning an attack on the president or event.Taele was charged with several felonies including second-degree robbery, receiving a large-capacity magazine and possession of a short-barreled rifle or shotgun. He was also charged with carrying a concealed firearm in a vehicle, a misdemeanor.He pleaded not guilty to all the charges Monday and was ordered to stay away from the golf course and not possess weapons. His bail was set at $250,000.It wasn’t clear if he had an attorney, and family members could not immediately be reached for comment.The sheriff’s department said when they made contact with Taele on Sunday, they had determined he was being investigated by the El Segundo Police Department for robbery.The sheriff's department said there is “no credible threat to our communities.”A jury in 2025 found a man guilty of trying to assassinate Trump at the president’s Florida country club.

news.title: Iran, Oman near Strait of Hormuz reopening deal amid US sanctions talks
news.text: Iran and Oman are moving closer to an agreement to reopen the disputed Strait of Hormuz, a key shipping route that has been hit by months of conflict. Under the emerging plan, ships would enter the Persian Gulf through a route controlled by Iran and leave through one controlled by Oman, according to two regional officials. Any agreement appears to depend on the United States lifting its blockade on Iranian ports, even as the Trump administration has earlier ruled out any deal that would give Iran control over the strait.Across the wider region on Tuesday, ships came under attack in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, Gaza City saw a mass funeral for more than 100 victims of an Israeli strike from early in the war, Israeli and Lebanese officials held talks in Rome on military withdrawal from southern Lebanon, Yemen’s Houthis claimed a strike on a Saudi airport, and families in Beirut marked six years since the 2020 port explosion.Senior US officials indicated that a deal on the strait could come soon. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there had been progress in talks between Iran and Oman, "but not finality yet". Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC that "there is a chance we may have a deal today or tomorrow to open the strait and move towards a more normalised position in this conflict".The Strait of Hormuz, at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, is a vital waterway through which a fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas passed before the war. It has effectively been shut by Iran’s attacks on shipping since the war began in February. Qatar’s emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, said he also spoke to US President Donald Trump on Tuesday as Qatar tried to help broker a resolution. Al Thani’s office said the two discussed ways to bridge the divide "in a way that enhances the prospects of reaching a sustainable diplomatic settlement to the crisis".A cargo ship reported being "hit by an unknown projectile" while passing through the Strait of Hormuz, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre. The centre said the strike damaged the vessel at around 2 am local time when it was about 37 kilometres northeast of Al Khasab, an Omani port city. It was not immediately clear which flag the ship was sailing under or whether it was carrying cargo, but British maritime security firm Ambrey also said it had sustained damage.In the Red Sea, an Indian-flagged commercial ship sank off Yemen after being hit by an explosive-laden boat, according to Yemeni and Indian authorities. Yemen’s coast guard rescued the crew, which included 13 Indians and one Yemeni. India’s Foreign Ministry condemned the attack. No group immediately claimed responsibility, though Iran-backed Houthi militants have repeatedly targeted ships travelling through the Red Sea near Yemen.In Gaza City, hundreds gathered as bodies wrapped in Palestinian flags were laid out in rows near flattened buildings before being carried on stretchers through a narrow street to a nearby cemetery. The 112 victims were among more than 300 people killed in an attack on the Sabra neighbourhood on November 22, 2023. First responders recovered the bodies over the weekend, including those of 40 children and 30 women, according to the Civil Defence, a rescue agency under Gaza’s Hamas-run Interior Ministry.The Gaza war began on October 7, 2023, when Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel, killing around 1,200 people and taking 251 hostage. Since then, Israel’s military offensive in Gaza has killed 73,375 people, including civilians and combatants, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. Another 7,400 people are still missing and are believed to be buried under the rubble, according to Zaher al-Waheidi, head of the ministry’s records department.Israeli and Lebanese officials met in Rome to continue talks on a US-mediated deal to reduce the Israeli military presence in southern Lebanon and disarm the Iran-backed Hezbollah group. A diplomat familiar with the negotiations said Lebanon had asked for the next "pilot zone" to be either Khiam or Bint Jbeil, both of which saw heavy fighting in the latest Israel-Hezbollah war and are now occupied by Israeli forces. But US Ambassador to Lebanon Michel Issa said before the three-day talks that no new pilot zones would be introduced immediately, warning that "moving too quickly risks jeopardizing the very civilians this process is meant to protect". Implementation of the June 26 agreement began last month with an initial pilot zone in an area that was not occupied by Israeli forces but had previously come under Israeli fire.In Yemen, Brig Gen Yahya Saree, a military spokesman for the Iranian-backed Houthis, said a drone hit a "sensitive target" at the airport in Najran in south-western Saudi Arabia, though he gave no evidence. He said the attack was in response to what he described as Saudi violations of Yemen’s airspace over Saada and Hajjah. There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia. The Houthis recently announced a blockade on Saudi-linked shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Saudi Arabia had led an international coalition and imposed an air and sea blockade after the rebels seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen in the civil war that began in 2014. Major fighting ended in a truce in 2022.In Beirut, families of more than 200 people killed in the 2020 port explosion gathered at the blast site to mark six years since improperly stored ammonium nitrate exploded and devastated large parts of the Lebanese capital. No one has been convicted in the long-delayed investigation, though some families said they were hopeful after government officials promised indictments by the end of the year. Tuesday’s developments reflected a region still shaped by war, stalled negotiations and unresolved tragedies, with the proposed Strait of Hormuz deal standing out as a possible opening in the wider conflict.With PTI Inputs- EndsPublished By: India Today Web Desk Published On: Aug 5, 2026 07:20 IST

news.title: Heavily armed man arrested at Trump's California golf course two days before planned fundraiser
news.text:
A heavily armed California man has been arrested at Donald Trump's Los Angeles-area golf course after allegedly taking photos and monitoring security preparations two days before the President was scheduled to host a major fundraising event. 

The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department confirmed that 38-year-old Jeanine John Taele was detained on Sunday at the Trump National Golf Course in Rancho Palos Verdes.

Deputies initially approached Taele after he was observed wandering the property, taking photos, and appearing to monitor security planning activities ahead of Tuesday’s Republican National Committee dinner.

Upon searching the suspect, law enforcement discovered a 16-round magazine filled with hollow-point ammunition in his pocket.

A further inspection of his vehicle revealed a loaded pistol alongside additional ammunition.

Following his initial arrest, law enforcement executed a search warrant on Monday at Taele’s residence in nearby Downey, California. 

Investigators recovered an illegally modified AR-style rifle, body armor, multiple high-capacity magazines, extensive rounds of ammunition, and notebooks containing what officials described as "concerning statements."

The sheriff’s department noted that Taele was also under active investigation by the El Segundo Police Department in connection with a separate robbery investigation.

“There is no credible threat to our communities,” the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department stated in a public advisory following the arrest.

Taele was formally charged with several offenses, including possession of a short-barreled rifle or shotgun, receiving a large-capacity magazine, carrying a concealed firearm in a vehicle, and second-degree robbery.

Appearing in court on Monday, Taele pleaded not guilty to all charges. A judge ordered him held on $250,000 bail and issued a protective order barring him from possessing firearms or approaching the golf course property.

The incident comes amid heightened security protocols surrounding presidential visits and events at private properties across the country.

Timeline of Donald Trump's assassination attempts

The president has been involved in a number of security-related incidents since taking office for the second time, including assassination attempts during his presidency and election campaigns.

July 2024 – Trump shot at Pennsylvania rally

Trump narrowly escaped death by just seconds as he was shot in the ear at a rally during his 2024 election campaign in Butler County.

At least five gunshots were fired as Secret Service agents rushed onto the stage to shield him from the attack.

The shooter was later identified as Thomas Matthew Crooks, 20, of Bethel Park, Pennsylvania, who was quickly shot dead by federal officers.

September 2024 – Second assassination attempt

It was September 15 when Trump was at his Florida golf resort around 2pm, when gunshots were heard as he moved between holes with Steve Witkoff, the US special envoy to the Middle East.

The course was swiftly locked down after Secret Service agents spotted a gun in nearby bushes and opened fire.

The suspect, Ryan Wesley Routh, was later arrested and, in February, was sentenced to life in prison for plotting to kill Trump.

September 2025 – Policeman infiltrates Trump’s security team

Melvin Eng, an off-duty New York Police Department officer, showed up at the Ryder Cup at Bethpage Black Course in tactical gear, allegedly posing as part of Trump’s security.

The policeman was on sick leave with no assignment, but was subsequently suspended pending investigation following the alarming behavior.

February 2026 – Gunman killed after crashing security perimeter at Trump's home

A man armed with a gas can and shotgun was shot dead by Secret Service agents after crashing into the security perimeter at Mar-a-Lago, while Trump was in Washington.

The attacker was identified as 21-year-old Austin Tucker Martin, from North Carolina, but his motive remains unclear.

April 2026 - An armed intruder infiltrates the White House Correspondent's Dinner

At the 2026 White House Correspondent's Dinner - the first attended by Trump while President, an armed intruder interrupted the proceedings just minutes into the event, as five gunshots echoed throughout the ballroom at the Hilton hotel, prompting an emergency evacuation of the President, senior cabinet officials, and finally the ultimate cancelling of the entire evening.

Addressing members of the press after the ordeal, Trump was asked directly how he felt in the moment, as this is the third time a shooting has taken place in his vicinity.

“It’s always shocking when something like this happens. It’s happened to me a little bit. The fact we were sitting right next to each other, and the First Lady on my right, and I heard a noise and thought it was a tray. I thought it was a tray going down - I’ve heard that many times - it was a pretty loud noise, and it was from pretty far away.

“He hadn’t breached the area at all before we got him. It was quite far away - but it was a gun. Some people really understood that pretty quickly, others didn’t. I was watching to see what was happening, but probably should’ve gone down even faster.”

Authorities identified the suspect as 31-year-old Cole Tomas Allen, who allegedly intended to target multiple Trump administration officials.

He was formally charged with federal gun crimes and attempting to assassinate Trump.

The gun charges include using a firearm during a crime of violence and interstate transportation of a firearm with intent to commit a felony.

Allen pleaded not guilty to all federal charges brought against him.

news.title: The One Move That Could Expose Democratic Hypocrisy on Supreme Court Reform
news.text:
"I know this is going to be controversial coming from me in particular — we need to revisit the Electoral College," Harris said, drawing applause from an audience that apparently didn't pause to ask why the loser of an election should get to redesign the rules of the next one.

She kept going. "We need to revisit the point of expanding the court to 13 justices like we have 13 District Courts," Harris said. "We need to revisit, if they so want, statehood for Puerto Rico and D.C."

Harris wants Democrats to become "too big to rig," a phrase she borrowed straight from Donald Trump's 2024 campaign. "It means being ruthless — they are ruthless," she said of Republicans.

Then came the part where Harris tried to have it both ways. "We need to be ruthless too, and by that, I do not mean cruel. That is not our nature. By that I do not mean breaking the law. That is not what we do," she said. "But I do mean we must be uncompromising, and we must allow for a real conversation about revisiting certain things."

🚨 Kamala reveals her 2028 agenda:1. Eliminate the Electoral College2. Pack the Supreme Court to 133. DC & Puerto Rican statehood pic.twitter.com/Pug2quL2KS— End Wokeness (@EndWokeness) July 31, 2026

Ruthless, but polite about it. Got it.

ICYMI: Another Trump Assassination Attempt May Have Just Been Thwarted

I have said countless times that Democrats will never stop trying their power grabs. Republicans might as well beat them to the punch and force Democrats on the record to explain why adding justices to the Supreme Court counts as restoring democracy rather than engineering a permanent majority.

The Electoral College is safe for now. Nixing it would require a constitutional amendment, and good luck with that. The number of justices on the Supreme Court, though, is set by Congress, not the Constitution, which makes Harris's 13-justice proposal something reasonably achievable. Joe Biden nearly tried it. The next time Democrats control the White House and Congress, they will try again.

And… according to Kamala Harris, there is a legitimate reason to set the number of justices to 13 because there are 13 federal District Courts. Okay, so let’s do it now. Right? If Democrats truly think 13 is the new magic number, Republicans should offer to help make it happen now, if only to get Democrats on record opposing it while a Republican is president. After all, setting the number of justices to the number of districts is important, right?

Make no mistake about it, ambition, not principle, explains the Democrats' enthusiasm for adding justices to the Supreme Court. It’s just a power grab, so let’s get them to admit it by opposing it when the timing isn’t politically convenient for them.

Democrats treat institutions as roadblocks only when it's convenient. They loved the filibuster when it blocked George W. Bush's judicial nominees, calling it a vital tool for the minority party. The moment Republicans used the same tool against Barack Obama's nominees, Democrats rebranded it a relic of Jim Crow and nuked it without a second thought.

In fact, I would add that Republicans should offer two bills: one to set the number of Supreme Court justices to 13, and the other to codify the number at nine. Let’s see how that plays out.

news.title: Jeremy Moss wins Democratic primary in 11th District: Reports
news.text:
Michigan Sen. Jeremy Moss, D-Southfield, won the Democratic primary for Michigan's 11th Congressional District, according to CNN and NBC. 

As of 9:36 p.m., Moss had 49.2% of the vote in a four-way contest that also included attorney Aisha Farooqi, Waterford School District trustee John Paul Torres and retired engineer Don Ufford. 

Moss will face Troy Mayor Ethan Baker in the general election in November. Baker ran unopposed in the Republican primary. 

In November, Moss will be heavily favored. Two political handicapping sites, Cook Political Report and Inside Elections, both rate the 11th District as a solidly Democratic seat. The district is based almost entirely in Oakland County. 

U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Birmingham, vacated the seat to run for U.S. Senate. In 2024, she won reelection by nearly 19 percentage points — a notable margin for the district's partisan makeup, given Republican President Donald Trump carried the state that year. 

Moss has been a state senator since 2019, having served two terms in the Michigan House prior to that. From 2011 to 2015, he was on Southfield's city council. 

In the Senate, he chairs the Elections and Ethics Committee as well as the Regulatory Affairs Committee. He is also President Pro Tempore, meaning he leads Senate sessions when Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist II is not in attendance. 

If elected, he would be Michigan's first openly gay member of Congress. 

Baker was first elected to Troy City Council in 2015 and has been mayor since 2019. Outside of his work with the city, Baker is an attorney specializing in estate planning, business law and real estate, according to his city bio. 

Baker is also an elected Republican precinct delegate and was a special assistant to former President Ronald Reagan and First Lady Nancy Reagan after they left the White House in 1990.

news.title: Netanyahu says IDF will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas has fully disarmed
news.text:
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says the Israeli military will not withdraw from its current lines in Gaza until Hamas has completely disarmed, pushing back against a recent deal announced by US President Donald Trump.

Mr Netanyahu's remarks cast more doubt on the deal to disarm Hamas, which was seen as a potential breakthrough for ending the war, and also marked a rare public display of friction between the Israeli government and the Trump administration.

The agreement called for Hamas to begin disarming and for Israel to halt its strikes and begin withdrawing from the roughly 60 per cent of Gaza it currently controls.

It was based on an October ceasefire agreement, which ended major military operations and brought about the release of the remaining hostages held in Gaza, but has since stalled on other fronts.

Speaking after a meeting with officials from Mr Trump's "Board of Peace", which negotiated the new deal, Mr Netanyahu reiterated his stance that Hamas's disarmament should come first, adding that Israeli forces would continue to "do whatever is necessary to protect themselves, our territory, and our citizens".

The US-backed ceasefire agreement last October called for Hamas to be disarmed and for Israel to withdraw.

An International Stabilisation Force was to be deployed, and an independent Palestinian administration was to oversee governance and reconstruction.

Israel now says everything hinges on Hamas giving up its weapons, while Hamas says Israel must end its strikes and begin withdrawing from the territory before it disarms.

Each side also accuses the other of violating the truce. At least 1,252 people — mostly women and children — have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire took effect, according to the territory's health ministry.

The ministry, part of the Hamas-led government, maintains detailed casualty records that are seen as generally reliable by UN agencies and independent experts, although they do not distinguish between civilian and militant deaths.

Israel says its strikes target militants who endanger its soldiers, took part in the October 7, 2023 terror attack or carry out other violations. Five Israeli soldiers have also been killed since the ceasefire took hold.

In the meantime, Gaza remains largely shattered.

Most of its 2 million Palestinians are displaced, many living in tent camps where poor conditions and overcrowding have led to rodent infestations and outbreaks of infectious diseases such as chickenpox.

Jordan sounds alarm over 'imminent' threat to Al-Aqsa mosque

Elsewhere in the Middle East, the neighbouring kingdom of Jordan has called an emergency meeting of Arab and Islamic foreign ministers for Wednesday, in response to what it says could be an "imminent" Israeli takeover of the Al-Aqsa mosque.

The meeting will bring together representatives from Arab League countries as well as Turkey, Indonesia, Malaysia and Pakistan, according to the Jordanian government.

It was prompted by a series of recent incursions by right-wing Israeli groups onto the compound around the mosque and the Dome of the Rock, which is situated in Jerusalem but controlled by Jordan under the terms of an uneasy "status quo" treaty.

On July 23, more than 2,000 Jewish religious extremists — mostly settlers, led by Israeli government minister Itamar Ben-Gvir — entered the compound, which is considered the third-holiest site in the Muslim world, behind Masjid al-Haram and the Prophet's Mosque in Saudi Arabia.

It is also considered the most important place in Judaism, although Israel's chief rabbinate and most ultra-orthodox rabbis say Jews should refrain from praying inside the compound (which they call the Temple of the Mount) on the grounds of Jewish religious law.

In addition to the Israeli incursions, there have been reports Israeli leaders are recruiting hardline religious Jews to form a Temple Mount police unit, while the pro-Qatari news outlet Middle East Eye reported in May that the US and Israel were "actively working" towards stripping Jordan of its custodianship of the compound in favour of an Israeli body that would institute a "multi-faith" approach.

Jordan's move to call a foreign ministers' meeting was first reported by The Guardian, which spoke to Foreign Minister Ayman Sadafi about his concerns ahead of a number of major Jewish holidays in September and a contentious Israeli election in October, in which Mr Netanyahu and his far-right coalition will be fighting to stay in office.

"Jerusalem is a tinderbox. We're trying to explain the danger."
news.summary: Benjamin Netanyahu's remarks are intended to push back against a recent deal to disarm Hamas announced by US President Donald Trump, which was seen as a potential breakthrough for ending the war.

news.title: US revokes visa of Brazilian ambassador to Washington
news.text: WASHINGTON, D.C. — The United States has revoked the visa of Brazil's ambassador, a State Department official said Tuesday, in a mounting diplomatic row just months before elections in Latin America's largest nation.The move would be reversed, the official said on customary condition of anonymity, if Brazil granted its approval of President Donald Trump's nominee to be ambassador Brasilia.Trump nominated Daniel Perez, a prominent Florida Republican, as the new ambassador to Brazil in early June.While the nomination still requires confirmation by the US Senate, he would not be able to take up the post until Brazil gives approval.'We think the government of Brazil owes us a prompt and positive answer to our request,' the official said.Brazil's envoy, Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti, was however not being declared persona non grata and forced to leave the United States, the official clarified.Brasilia responded swiftly and condemned the US move as an escalation of a diplomatic standoff.'Today's decision is not an isolated incident. It is part of a deliberate escalation of hostile measures against Brazil, motivated by ideological reasons,' the office of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said in a statement.The latest spat comes just months before Brazil holds a presidential election in October, with leftist incumbent Lula facing a challenge from right-wing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro.Brazil also recently denied visas for two US officials who sought to meet with election authorities last month, a Brazilian diplomatic source said, citing the 'risk of political exploitation.'A US State Department spokesperson said at the time that the two officials wanted to visit Brasilia to discuss 'election integrity, religious freedom and freedom of expression' with government officials, religious leaders and others.'Any insinuation of a 'ploy' to undermine a democratic nation's election is a baseless lie,' the spokesperson said.Brazil's denial of the visas came after Flavio Bolsonaro renewed unfounded claims that the country's electronic voting system was insecure, and as Trump continues to falsely claim that widespread fraud cost him a 2020 electoral win.In 2023, Bolsonaro's father, ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, was barred by electoral authorities from running for office after he raised similar claims the year prior, while still in the presidency.He was later convicted for plotting a coup following his 2022 election loss and is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest.

news.title: Rep. Wesley Bell defeats former Rep. Cori Bush in St. Louis' 1st Congressional District primary
news.text: U.S. Rep. Wesley Bell won a rematch Tuesday in a Democratic primary against former U.S. Rep. Cori Bush, and Missouri voters rejected a ballot measure that could have made ii harder to pass citizen-led amendments in the future.Bell’s primary victory is likely to propel him to reelection in November in the heavily Democratic 1st Congressional District in St. Louis.Bell, a former St. Louis County prosecutor, was backed by a political group affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. The pro-Israeli group also financed his ouster of Bush in the 2024 primary after Bush criticized Israel’s response in Gaza to Hamas’ attack on Israel in 2023.Bush had been a part of a progressive group of House members known as the Squad.The rematch was one of several consequential primaries. Another amendment under consideration would direct lawmakers to repeal the state’s individual income tax while authorizing a state sales tax expansion.St. Louis primary pits Israel critic against supporterThe contest between Bush and Bell tested how much the Democratic Party has shifted over the past two years.The deep-pocketed American Israel Public Affairs Committee spent millions to help oust Bush in 2024. Bell was again supported by AIPAC.But public opinions of Israel have since shifted, particularly among Democrats. A recent survey by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that about 58% of Democrats now say the U.S. is “too supportive” of Israelis, up from 45% in an AP-NORC poll from January 2024.This year's primary also tested the clout of democratic socialists, who traveled from across the country to help campaign for Bush.Bush and Bell both honed their leadership skills in Ferguson amid the racial unrest that followed the fatal shooting of Michael Brown by a police officer in 2014. A six-person Republican primary features state Sen. Rick Brattin, a Marine veteran and founding member of the Missouri Freedom Caucus, a conservative faction that has challenged the legislature’s GOP leadership. Brattin now has the backing of some of Missouri's top Republicans, including Gov. Mike Kehoe, and received an endorsement from Trump on the evening before the election.His main advertising competitor has been Taylor Burks, a Navy officer who previously served as Boone County clerk, which oversees elections in the home county of the University of Missouri.Retirement creates an opening for a Republican-held seatGraves, who has represented rural northern Missouri for a quarter century, set off a political scramble when he announced in late March that he wasn’t seeking reelection. He endorsed conservative talk radio host Chris Stigall, who once worked for Graves.The five-person Republican field in the GOP-leaning 6th District also features Kansas City Council member Nathan Willett. The recent redistricting added more northern Kansas City neighborhoods to the sprawling district. The Democratic primary has three candidates.
news.summary: U.S. Rep. Wesley Bell won a rematch Tuesday in a Democratic primary against former U.S. Rep. Cori Bush.

news.title: Brazil cuts Argentina diplomatic presence after Milei renews attacks on Lula
news.text: Brazil said on Tuesday that it is further reducing its diplomatic presence in Argentina after Argentine President Javier Milei renewed his attacks on Brazilian President Luiz Incio Lula da Silva. The move marks the first such step between the neighbouring countries in recent history.The latest escalation comes after Milei again referred to Lula in offensive terms, deepening a relationship that has remained tense since the Argentine leader took office in December 2023. Brazil has said its ambassador to Buenos Aires will not return while such remarks continue.A spokesperson for Brazil's foreign office told The Associated Press that Milei has called Lula "a thief" three times since Sunday. The spokesperson said Milei had used similar language on July 25 at the party convention of Senator Flvio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who will be Lula's rival in October's election.At the same convention, Milei also described Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes as "trash". De Moraes had denied Milei's request to visit former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest and serving a 27-year sentence for a coup attempt.Brazil recalled its ambassador to Buenos Aires, Julio Bitelli, in July, a day after Milei's first remarks against Lula. Since then, Brazil's interests in Argentina have been handled by a charg d'affaires, a lower-ranked diplomatic post. The spokesperson said Bitelli will not return to Argentina as long as Milei continues to make aggressive comments about Lula.Lula has not commented on Milei's latest remarks. Milei is a close ally of US President Donald Trump, whose administration is at odds with Lula. Vice President Geraldo Alckmin, a conservative who will again be Lula's running mate, said Brazil's electronic voting system was so effective that "it does not accept any votes from Argentines and Americans", referring to Milei and Trump.In sum, Brazil has decided to scale back its diplomatic presence in Argentina as tensions rise over Milei's repeated attacks on Lula, adding to a wider strain involving the two neighbours and the United States ahead of Brazil's election.With PTI Inputs- EndsPublished By: India Today Web Desk Published On: Aug 5, 2026 07:02 IST

news.title: Oil steadies after two-day slump as investors eye Hormuz traffic
news.text:
PERTH, Aug 5 : Oil steadied on Wednesday after steep falls in the previous two trading sessions, as investors waited to see if efforts to end the U.S.-Iran war and restore traffic through the blockaded Strait of Hormuz were making progress.

Brent crude futures rose 26 cents, or about 0.33 per cent, to $79.62 a barrel by 0110 GMT. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures rose 0.16 per cent, or 12 cents, to $75.90 a barrel. 

Qatar said on Tuesday mediators were making progress in efforts to end the war, driving oil prices lower, although Tehran has denied U.S. President Donald Trump's assertion that talks are already under way. Brent closed on Tuesday below $80 a barrel for the first time since July 13. 

“The main sticking point appears to be whether Iran will continue to insist on a degree of control over the waterway, and whether the U.S. will stand its ground and refuse that outcome,” analysts from IG said in a note.

Brent closed more than 5 per cent lower on Tuesday after the comments from Qatar, extending Monday's steep losses on hopes that an arrangement could soon be reached. Prior to the beginning of the war some 20 per cent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas transited through the strait, and in March alone prices rose 50 per cent. 

Trump and Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani discussed efforts to narrow differences between Washington and Tehran and improve the prospects for a lasting settlement during a phone call on Tuesday, Qatar's Emiri office said.

Trump said on Monday that talks with Tehran had started and Iran faced a "last chance" to reach a deal. Iranian officials insisted no negotiations with the U.S. were taking place.

U.S. crude and gasoline inventories rose while distillate stocks fell last week, market sources said on Tuesday, citing data from the American Petroleum Institute.

Crude stocks rose by about 2.7 million barrels in the week ended July 31, the sources said on condition of anonymity.

Official numbers from the EIA, the statistical arm of the U.S. Department of Energy, are due at 10:30 a.m. ET (1430 GMT) on Wednesday.

news.title: Trump's UFC Freedom 250 Fight Reportedly Lost Staggering Amount Of Money
news.text:
President Donald Trump’s controversial UFC Freedom 250 event at the White House South Lawn earlier this summer reportedly cost the mixed martial arts company millions.

Despite generating widespread attention, the event cost the UFC approximately $30 million, per a report from BBC Sport. UFC was able to recoup some of the event’s costs, which were initially estimated to be $60 million, through sponsorships and media partnerships. 

Andrew Schleimer, chief financial officer of UFC’s parent company told BBC Sport the fight incurred significantly higher than normal costs. 

“Given the event’s profile, which as anticipated, resulted in an approximate $30m loss, our margins at UFC as well as on a consolidated basis were meaningfully impacted,” Schleimer said.

UFC president Dana White had predicted the event’s viewership would somehow rival that of the Super Bowl, and Trump bragged after the fight that it might have been more important than the FIFA World Cup. Ultimately, the event drew 34 million viewers, roughly one-fourth of February’s Super Bowl LX. 

The much-maligned event, held on Trump’s 80th birthday, was a hodgepodge of patriotic symbolism, including ring walkouts that began inside the White House. 

The fight also drew widespread criticism after heavyweight Josh Hokit randomly blurted out “Michelle Obama is a man” during his post-fight interview. The comments were eventually condemned by White.

DUBAI, United Arab Emirates (AFP)—The United States was hopeful that a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz would be done “today or tomorrow”, a top official said Tuesday, sending oil prices tumbling on optimism for increased shipments in the vital waterway.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told broadcaster CNBC “there is a chance we may have a deal” in the coming hours, echoing remarks from President Donald Trump the day before.

Speaking from the White House on Monday, Trump kept up his now familiar combination of optimism for diplomacy and bellicose threats, warning that this was Iran’s “last chance before decapitation”.

Tehran and Washington have been at war since February 28, when the US and Israel launched surprise attacks on Iran. Despite a ceasefire and a preliminary deal in the months since, diplomacy has failed to end the conflict.

Underlining the fragility of the situation, one crew member was listed missing Tuesday on a merchant ship hit by a projectile in Hormuz, with fire erupting in the accommodation area.

The Strait of Hormuz, a key conduit for global oil and gas supplies, has been the spark for repeated returns to fighting.

Iran wants to maintain control over and charge tolls in the strait, powers it did not exercise before the war and which the US fiercely opposes.

In what has become a regular pattern, Trump last week threatened to hit Iran “very hard”, potentially with attacks against civilian infrastructure, only to pull back later, hinting that a deal was near.

But Iran’s foreign ministry denied negotiations with Washington were taking place, even as Trump insisted they were happening “right now”.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday that the United States was involved in negotiations between Oman and Iran on increasing traffic through the Hormuz.

“There’s been progress made in those talks but not finality yet. We’re hoping that will happen very shortly,” he told journalists.

The closure of the Hormuz has rattled global markets, and rekindled hopes for its reopening drove benchmark Brent North Sea Crude prices down nearly five percent to $79.69 per barrel on Tuesday.

– Deal or surrender –

Qatar, which has been mediating negotiations, said that diplomatic efforts were ongoing but that no direct Iran-US talks were planned.

Its leader, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, spoke with Trump by phone on Tuesday, with the emir’s palace saying they discussed “efforts to de-escalate tensions between the United States of America and the Islamic Republic of Iran and to bring the two sides closer together”.

Trump had previously said he expected to know by Tuesday how the talks were going, “one way or the other”, but insisted “it’s not very complex”.

Washington’s diplomatic goals include reopening Hormuz and the denuclearisation of Iran, which Trump allowed could “take a little while”.

The president had previously called Tehran “duplicitous” for saying it was not negotiating, adding on social media that a US counter-blockade of Iranian ports would stay in place “unless a Deal, or Total Surrender, is accomplished”.

More than five months into a war that has cost Washington billions of dollars, Iran remains able to fire missiles and drones at US and allied targets in the region, as well as at commercial shipping.

Early on Tuesday, Britain’s maritime security agency UKMTO said an unnamed cargo vessel had been struck by an “unknown projectile” in the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Oman.

Iran continues to impose an effective blockade on the strait and insists ships coordinate crossings with it.

– Red Sea attack –

The disruptions in the Hormuz have only placed greater importance on shipping lanes through the Red Sea, where Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia.

The Saudi Red Sea port of Yanbu has enabled it to keep up shipments to global markets by circumventing the Hormuz entirely.

But since the Houthis announced their blockade, they have claimed attacks on multiple ships they say are in violation.

On Tuesday, the Indian ship MSV Faize Noore Oliya sank in the Red Sea off Yemen following an unattributed attack, with all of its crew rescued, according to India’s foreign ministry and a local official in Yemen.

“The targeting of commercial shipping in the region must end,” a foreign ministry spokesperson said.

The Red Sea is a gateway to the Suez Canal, and a previous campaign of Houthi attacks on commercial vessels during the Gaza war made passage through the strategic shortcut increasingly untenable, prompting many shippers to instead take lengthy detours around the southern tip of Africa.

news.title: Trump admin revokes visa of Brazil’s ambassador to US as payback
news.text:
The Trump administration has revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the United States in retaliation for Brazil’s denial of visas last month for two American diplomats who sought to visit ahead of upcoming elections as well as Brazil’s stalling on approving President Donald Trump’s nominee to be ambassador in Brasilia.

The State Department said the decision was a reciprocal response to Brazil’s actions and officials said the step had been delayed several times to give Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva room to back down, something he did not do. Officials said, however, that it could be quickly reversed if Brazil takes appropriate action and accepts Trump’s ambassadorial choice.

Trump has had a fractious relationship for some time with Lula’s administration, which has opposed him on numerous policies, particularly in the Western Hemisphere regarding Venezuela and Cuba. Their relationship also has been strained by Trump’s fondness for Lula’s first term successor and then predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro, who is currently under house arrest, and his son Flavio, who is Lula’s main opponent in October election.

Despite the revocation of her visa, Brazil’s ambassador Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti is not being expelled from the United States, said one State Department official, who like several others spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the sensitive diplomatic matter. The ambassador was previously a senior United Nations official.

She could be allowed to resume her official duties if the Brazilian government accepts Trump’s choice of former Florida House speaker Danny Perez to be U.S. ambassador to Brazil. Perez was nominated to the post in June and the official said Brazil had signaled it would not act on the appointment until after the October election.

In addition to stalling on Perez, Brazil denied visas last month for Riley Barnes, the assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights and labor, and one of his top aides after reports emerged that the pair were going to criticize Lula or the election process.

The State Department denied the allegations and said the two had planned to visit Brasilia on July 27-30 to meet government officials, religious leaders and others about “election integrity,” religious freedom and freedom of expression.

It said the visit was routine and that “any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie.”

Brazil’s government did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press about the revocation of the ambassador’s visa, but last week a top Brazilian diplomat told journalists the government was expecting a response from the U.S.

The diplomat also mentioned the U.S. government had triggered the proceedings to send Perez to Brasilia before seeking Brazil’s approval, which is different from standard diplomatic procedure. The diplomat spoke on condition of anonymity due to lack of authorization to discuss the matter publicly.

Lula will face Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, whose father once served as Brazil’s president and whose family has many ties with the Trump administration, in the Oct. 4 polls. The administration has numerous issues with Lula and his policies and has also hosted the younger Bolsonaro, who is seeking to carry on his father’s conservative governance.

Sen. Bolsonaro and his brother, Eduardo, visited U.S. officials in Washington, including Trump, in late May. Shortly afterward, the Trump administration classified Brazil’s biggest drug-trafficking groups — First Command Capital and Red Command — as foreign terrorist organizations, a move Lula opposes.

The Trump administration also imposed an up to 37.5% tariff hike on thousands of Brazilian exports, which came into force Friday. The U.S. government claims the South American nation has unfair competition practices and fails to stop forced labor practices — both accusations rejected by the Lula administration as an attempt to sway the election to Sen. Bolsonaro.

Jair Bolsonaro has for years fed concerns about the country’s electronic voting system, without providing any evidence for his claims. He is now serving a 27-year prison sentence at home for an attempted coup. He has long insisted that the machines, used for a quarter-century, are prone to fraud.

His son, Sen. Bolsonaro, has recently repeated some of these claims, although he steered clear of those on Saturday when his Liberal Party confirmed him as a presidential candidate in Sao Paulo.
news.summary: The Trump administration revoked the visa of Brazil's ambassador, Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti, in retaliation for blocked US diplomat visas.
news.author: Associated Press
