news.title: Armed man arrested outside Trump's Los Angeles golf course before presidential visit
news.text:
A man carrying ammunition and with a gun in his car was arrested Sunday at President Donald Trump’s Los Angeles-area golf course after appearing to monitor security preparations two days ahead of Trump’s fundraiser there, authorities said Tuesday.

The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department said Jeanine John Taele, 38, was taking photos and video and had a 16-round magazine with ammunition in his pocket. Authorities recovered a loaded pistol in his car. Law enforcement searched his home in the nearby city of Downey on Monday and found a plethora of firearms, magazines and ammunition, body armor and notebooks with “concerning statements.”

The sheriff’s department announced the arrest as Trump was preparing to arrive for a fundraising dinner for the Republican National Committee at the Trump National Golf Course in the suburb of Rancho Palos Verdes just south of Los Angeles.

Taele was charged with several felonies including second-degree robbery, receiving a large-capacity magazine and possession of a short-barreled rifle or shotgun. He was also charged with carrying a concealed firearm in a vehicle, a misdemeanor.

He pleaded not guilty to all the charges Monday and was ordered to stay away from the golf course and not possess weapons. His bail was set at $250,000.

It wasn’t clear if he had an attorney, and family members could not immediately be reached for comment.

The sheriff’s department said when they made contact with Taele on Sunday, they had determined he was being investigated by the El Segundo Police Department for robbery.

The sheriff's department said there is “no credible threat to our communities.”

A jury in 2025 found a man guilty of trying to assassinate Trump at the president’s Florida country club.

(FRANCE 24 with AP)
news.summary: Authorities arrested a man carrying ammunition and later found a loaded gun in his car outside US President Donald Trump's Los Angeles-area golf course, where he was allegedly photographing security preparations ahead of the US president's fundraising event.
news.author: FRANCE 24

news.title: FIFA boss accused of ‘blackmail’ amid panicked calls to Trump
news.text:
Gianni Infantino’s attempt to seek the support of US President Donald Trump has reportedly failed, as the FIFA boss prepares to host a crisis meeting in Morocco. 

Pressure has been mounting on Infantino since he announced he was abandoning his plan to sell a stake of the commercial rights of all major FIFA run competitions.

A number of member associations have spoken out against Infantino and withdrawn support for him as FIFA president. He is under siege and reportedly feeling “isolated”.

The New York Post revealed that in an attempt to save his job, Infantino has repeatedly tried to reach President Trump via a phone call for support. He has failed to get a response. 

The pair had formed a close relationship since it was announced the United States would be hosting the Club World Cup and the World Cup. 

Infantino and Trump have been seen at several major football events together. Trump even received the inaugural FIFA Peace Prize from the FIFA president last year. 

The Peace Prize raised concern within the football community and those fears have only grown after Trump’s ties to Infantino’s sell-off plan was revealed.

Infantino is set to run for election in a bid to retain his job as FIFA president in March next year, in what will be his final term if he is re-elected.

But to add to the list of dilemmas Infantino is now facing, FIFA has also been accused of blackmailing Jordan’s national team by withholding their prize money won during the FIFA Arab Cup that was played last December. 

Prince Ali bin Al Hussein, who served on FIFA’s executive committee from 2011-15, made the claim on X.

Prince Ali noted that FIFA has continued to “brag about how many billions they have in reserve” while his team waits for that payment. 

He also criticised the difficulty Jordan’s fans faced securing visas to watch their team debut at this year’s World Cup despite paying the “exorbitant ticket prices” and how the team was taxed by the US government via FIFA for competing in the event.

Due to those issues and Infantino’s failed sell-off plan, Prince Ali said he could not endorse Infantino as a leader any further. 

“For months, FIFA has been refusing to help us on any of these or other matters until it was verbally communicated to me during the World Cup that if I endorsed Infantino it would go a long way to helping our FA out,” he wrote on X. 

“It is clear the problem really is with leadership ... the whole situation amounts to blackmail, and we refuse to give in to that.”

The Athletic is also reporting that host cities from the FIFA Club World Cup last year are still waiting for their $1.4 million AUD payments promised by Infantino.

A request has been lodged by some host cities for an update on those payments.

It has been reported that FIFA generated a record-breaking $21b in revenue at the 2026 FIFA World Cup. 

The football world will eagerly await to see what the result of FIFA’s crisis meeting is on Wednesday (AEST). It is unclear if Infantino will resign or stay on, although there are vast calls for him to call time on his tenure as president.
news.author: Alyssa Bone

news.title: Police arrest armed man outside Trump’s golf course in California
news.text:
Aug. 4 (UPI) -- Deputies arrested an armed man Sunday outside Trump National Golf Club in Southern California, days before President Donald Trump's visit Tuesday, the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department announced.

Jeanine John Taele, 38, of Downey, Calif., pleaded guilty Tuesday to three weapons charges related to Sunday's arrest and a second-degree robbery charge from an alleged November incident, the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office said.

Plainclothes federal agents alerted sheriff's deputies to a "suspicious individual" on the golf club property in Rancho Palos Verdes, a Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department release said. The man was "observed walking through the golf course grounds taking photographs and videos and appearing to monitor security-planning activities."

Trump was scheduled to attend a Republican National Committee event at the golf course Tuesday night. He was on Air Force One on the way to California when the sheriff's department announced the arrest, CNN reported.

Deputies identified the suspect as Taele, who was already under investigation in a robbery case by the El Segundo Police Department. They detainedhim and found his vehicle in a parking lot for the course.

"During the detention, deputies recovered a 16-round magazine containing hollow-point ammunition from Taele's pants pockets," the release said. They "subsequently searched Taele's vehicle and recovered a loaded pistol with a round chambered, along with an additional loaded magazine containing hollow-point ammunition."

Taele was arrested on charges of carrying a concealed firearm and possession of prohibited ammunition.

Detectives from the FBI's Joint Terrorism Task Force then executed a search warrant for Taele's home Monday because of "the potential security implications surrounding the incident," the sheriff's department said.

There, they recovered what are described as an illegally modified AR platform rifle, body armor, a .45-caliber pistol, bulk pistol and rifle ammunition, two "radio signal devices," multiple notebooks containing "concerning statements" and other items.

The FBI Joint Terrorism Task Force and Secret Service are aiding the investigation. A judge set Taele's bail at $250,000, banned him from possessing weapons and ordered him to stay away from the golf club and to stay in California, CNN reported.

"Currently, investigators have identified no credible threat to our communities," the sheriff's department said. "However, this case underscores the importance of vigilance, strong partnerships with local, state and federal law enforcement agencies and the proactive steps taken to identify and investigate suspicious activity before it can escalate."
news.summary: Deputies arrested an armed man Sunday outside Trump National Golf Club in California, days before President Donald Trump's visit to the club Tuesday.
news.author: Jill Keppeler

news.title: Trump admin lands dozens of immigration detentions in trucking crackdown operation
news.text:
President Donald Trump’s administration announced the results of a crackdown on illegal immigration in the trucking industry Tuesday.

The Department of Transportation (DOT) began the crackdown, Operation Highway Shield, in Florida earlier this year. The DOT has since expanded the effort to multiple states in the Midwest, including Illinois, Indiana, Iowa and Ohio, Fox News has learned.

Officials carried out 3,487 enforcement stops during the operation that resulted in 766 unsafe commercial vehicles or drivers placed out of service, 51 immigration detentions, 47 criminal charges filed, 39 incarcerations, 36 English language proficiency (ELP) violations and three cargo theft recoveries totaling roughly $1 million in stolen freight.

The Trump administration maintains that federal immigration and commercial driving enforcement remains a top priority.

Fox News previously broke news about the ramped-up enforcement efforts in Florida in March. Florida troopers said up to half of truckers at some weigh stations cannot meet English proficiency requirements.

“I try to concentrate on the [signs] they have to read,” Master Trooper Craig Lents said at the time. “If you are going down the road at 70 miles per hour, and you see that sign, you only see it for a split second.”

In another encounter caught on video, a trooper asked a trucker what a road sign meant.

The trucker replied, “No.”

The trooper then asked what drivers should do if they saw the sign, to which the trucker replied, “No,” again.

The Trump administration has noted that federal English requirements have been on the books for years.

“It’s been the law for a long period of time,” said Derek Barrs, Federal Motor Carrier Safety administrator. “It’s a safety issue. … If there was a crash or something like that, I would want to make sure that driver would know how to respond — slow down for upcoming traffic or a crash that has happened up ahead.”

Authorities explained that being unable to speak or read English is dangerous because truckers are driving by important road signs at high speeds while carrying hundreds of tons.

The enforcement push comes after a string of deadly crashes nationwide involving drivers the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) claims were in the U.S. illegally or operating with commercial drivers’ licenses (CDLs) they should never have had.
news.summary: President Donald Trump's administration announced the results of a crackdown on illegal immigration in the trucking industry Tuesday.
news.author: Fox News

news.title: Why an Iran deal might happen this time despite mixed signals
news.text:
Oil traders are buying into the Trump administration’s latest claims that a deal is near with Iran, pushing both the international and U.S. benchmarks down sharply this week.

In Tuesday’s latest developments, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said there was “a chance” that a deal would be struck “today or tomorrow.” His comments come after President Donald Trump called off strikes on Iran over the weekend, claiming “perimeters of a deal” to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

The price of most-active futures for Brent crude oil and West Texas Intermediate were down about 5% each, respectively, by midday Tuesday. Brent was trading at $79.54, with WTI at $76.12.

While we’ve heard such optimistic talk many times before, only for hostilities to resume, a new report that the U.S. has depleted “virtually all” of its land-based, long-range tactical missiles, could explain at least some of the renewed optimism.

Reuters reported early Tuesday that the U.S. has nearly used up its surface-to-surface weapons, called Army Tactical MissileSystems (ATACMS) and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM). These are preferred over munitions dropped by jets or fired from the sea because they can be launched quickly and fired quickly to avoid detection.

When Barron’s asked the White House about the report, the press office provided earlier comments from President Trump and a spokesperson saying the U.S. has ample munitions, but didn’t specifically address the reported shortage of these specific missiles.

RBC Capital Markets head of global commodity strategy Helima Croft says the reported shortage could be putting more pressure on the administration to make a deal. “These munitions constraints may be incentivizing the White House to take a deal that seemingly meets Iran’s core demands for Hormuz control,” she said.

Despite Bessent signaling an imminent breakthrough, there were also signs of renewed fighting. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reported early Tuesday that a cargo vessel was struck by an unknown projectile as it was traversing Omani territorial waters in the Strait of Hormuz. It also reported threats to two oil tankers in the strait.

Meanwhile, TD Securities global head of commodity strategy Bart Melek calls the recent drop in oil prices “likely an inappropriate response on several fronts.” There is less oil loaded up on tankers and ready to pass through the strait than was when it last reopened in June, oil production is muted, and there is no indication that Iran is willing to give up control of the waterway.

“Given that prices have dropped sharply in recent days and a resolution to the conflict is not on the horizon, we expect both long exposure and prices to move up robustly in the coming week,” Melek wrote in a Tuesday note.

“Even an imminent opening of these seaways would not prevent a significant erosion of global inventories due to shipping lags, production stoppages,” he told Barron’s.

Write to Anita Hamilton at anita.hamilton@barrons.com
news.author: Anita Hamilton

news.title: CNN, AP: Jocelyn Benson wins Democratic primary for Michigan governor
news.text:
Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson won the Democratic primary race for governor, defeating Genesee County Sheriff Chris Swanson, according to CNN and the Associated Press.

As of 9:04 p.m. Tuesday, Aug. 4, Benson was leading with 85% of the vote with Swanson carrying 14%.

Benson has served as Michigan's chief elections officer since 2019. In the role, she has built a national profile for vigorously defending Michigan's 2020 election against efforts by President Donald Trump and his allies to overturn his loss. She has pitched herself as the candidate who can improve state bureaucracies to save residents time and money, pointing to her overhaul of Michigan's vehicle services to reduce wait times at Secretary of State branch offices.

Her campaign promises "to make Michigan the best place to be a kid, raise a kid, and call home."

Benson said her priorities, if elected, include expanding universal pre-K to 3-year-olds, allowing local governments to establish higher minimum wages than the one set by the state, and transforming support services at the Michigan Department of Health and Human services, which administers the state’s Medicaid and food assistance programs.

Usman Ibrahim, 52, of Rochester Hills, early voted on Aug. 1, supporting Benson in the gubernatorial contest.

"She's been in politics for a while, has her views known, and I think she would be good," he said. 

Since launching her campaign in January 2025, Benson had consistently outpaced Swanson in the polls and fundraising. (Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist II initially campaigned against Benson, but he dropped his bid to run for her current job instead.)

More: Michigan primary election updates: Polls closed, results trickle in

In the primary, Benson boasted endorsements from many Democratic state lawmakers along with reproductive rights groups. Labor unions were divided between Benson and Swanson, though the secretary of state notched some high-profile union support such as an endorsement from the UAW.

Gov. Gretchen Whitmer cannot run again due to term limits. The race to replace her is one of several competitive open races for governor across the United States.

Michigan voters have routinely flipped party control of the governor's office when replacing the outgoing leader. A victory for Benson in the fall would defy that pattern. At the same time, she appears poised to benefit from headwinds facing Republicans in the midterm election, which typically sees the current president’s party suffer losses.

Before serving as secretary of state, Benson was the dean of the Wayne State University Law School and the CEO of the Ross Initiative in Sports for Equality, a nonprofit started by Stephen Ross — the founder of the real estate firm Related Companies — focused on improving race relations in sports.

The general election will take place Tuesday, Nov. 3.

news.title: Susan Collins to vote against Todd Blanche's nomination for Attorney General, even as other Republicans back him
news.text: Susan Collins, the Republican senator from Maine, on Tuesday said she will vote against Todd Blanche as Attorney General, hours after his nomination cleared a key Senate vote."While I believe Mr. Blanche is a capable lawyer, the Department of Justice has become increasingly political," Collins said in a statement."Mr. Blanche has taken several actions that have further eroded the Department's independence, and that is the basis for my vote to oppose his confirmation," the statement added.Collins, who is up for reelection in a state Donald Trump lost in 2024, cited Blanche’s approval of a deal shielding Trump and his family from Internal Revenue Service audits, the creation of a $1.8 billion so-called anti-weaponization fund and a promise to an anti-abortion organization that he would seek to prohibit the mailing of abortion drugs as reasons for her opposition.Collins also said attempts to indict Democratic Senators Mark Kelly and Elissa Slotkin “over their ill-advised, but constitutionally protected, videos encouraging resistance to unlawful orders.”Todd Blanche gets more Republican supportEarlier, John Cornyn from Texas and Thom Tillis from North Carolina, the two Republicans who had initially opposed Blanche’s nomination over Trump's proposed $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund, agreed to support him after reaching a written agreement with the Acting USAG. They also said that Blanche agreed to narrow the scope of the IRS settlement's audit protections for Trump.Another Republican, John Curtis from Utah, who had previously indicated he had concerns about voting for Blanche, said Tuesday that he would also support him.Todd Blanche can't afford losing more votesThis has left just two Republicans - Bill Cassidy from Louisiana and Lisa Murkowski from Alaska who haven’t said how they will vote.All Democratic Senators are expected to oppose the nomination of Blanche, and with Mitch McConnell, who is recovering from a fall in June, still absent, the Trump nominee can only afford to lose two GOP votes.The Senate Judiciary Committee voted 12-10 along party lines in support of the nomination of President Donald Trump’s former personal attorney.Vice President JD Vance, in a post on X following the committee vote, said Blanche "will continue to serve the American people and the Trump Administration loyally, and he will make a great Attorney General."The full Senate, where Republicans hold a majority, is expected to vote later this week to confirm Blanche as attorney general. He has been serving as acting attorney general since Trump fired Pam Bondi in April.Prior to joining the Department of Justice, Blanche represented Trump in his New York trial over alleged "hush money" paid to porn star Stormy Daniels.He was also on the legal defense team in two federal cases brought against Trump by special counsel Jack Smith. Both cases were dropped after Trump won the 2024 presidential election.(With inputs from agencies)

news.title: Brazil cuts diplomatic presence in Argentina after Milei's attacks on Lula
news.text:
SAO PAULO (AP) — Brazil’s government on Tuesday announced it is reducing its diplomatic presence in Argentina after renewed attacks by Argentine President Javier Milei on his counterpart Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. 

It is the first time in recent history that such a move takes place between the two neighbors.

A spokesperson for Brazil’s foreign office told The Associated Press that Milei has called Lula “a thief” three times since Sunday. He used similar wording on July 25 at the party convention of Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president who will be Lula’s rival in October’s election. 

Milei also accused Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes of being “trash” during the convention. De Moraes denied a request by the Argentine president to visit former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest serving a 27-year sentence for a coup attempt.

The Brazilian government recalled its ambassador to Buenos Aires, Julio Bitelli, in July, a day after Milei’s first remarks against Lula. Since then, Brazil’s interests in Argentina are represented by a chargé d’affaires, a lower-ranked position.

Bitelli will not return to Argentina as long as Milei continues to make aggressive comments toward Lula, the spokesperson said. 

The Brazilian president has not commented on Milei’s remarks. The two have had a frosty relationship since the Argentine leader took office in December 2023.

Milei is a close ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, whose administration is at odds with Lula. Earlier on Tuesday, the U.S. State Department revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to Washington in retaliation for Brazil’s denial of visas last month for two American diplomats who sought to visit ahead of upcoming elections.

Lula was officially declared candidate for reelection Sunday at his Workers’ Party convention, where many voiced concerns of foreign interference in the country’s vote.

Vice President Geraldo Alckmin, a conservative who will once again be Lula’s running mate, said the country’s electronic voting system was so effective that “it doesn’t accept any votes from Argentines and Americans,” in a reference to Milei and Trump.

news.title: Rep. Wesley Bell defeats former Rep. Cori Bush in a Missouri Democratic primary rematch
news.text: ST. LOUIS — Rep. Wesley Bell defeated former Rep. Cori Bush in a Democratic primary rematch, NBC News projects, in the latest chapter of a long-term fight over a deep-blue, St. Louis-based district. Bell overwhelmed Bush on the airwaves, fending off her push to make the race a referendum on his support for U.S. aid to Israel. In total, Bell’s campaign and outside allies outspent Bush by a staggering 27-to-1 margin, according to AdImpact, an ad-tracking service. United Democracy Project — the super PAC linked to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the pro-Israel advocacy group known as AIPAC — spent $2 million to support Bell, largely through negative ads attacking Bush. One such ad slammed Bush for being critical of former Vice President Kamala Harris. It was a reference to Bush criticizing the Biden-Harris administration for supporting Israel amid what she deemed a genocide in Gaza. She endorsed Harris in the 2024 election. As Bell cast his vote Tuesday, he criticized Bush for focusing on Israel and talking “over and over is talking about an issue that is not impacting folks right here in St. Louis.” “And while we take those issues seriously, you know, the M in Missouri doesn’t stand for Middle East,” Bell told NBC News. “It stands for Missouri.” At a campaign stop later Tuesday, Bush hit back at Bell’s claims and said Missourians “are not happy” that he filled his “campaign coffers” with money from outside groups. “Why are they meddling in our primaries?” she asked. “Why does he allow that?” AIPAC loomed large in the race after helping Bell oust Bush two years ago. United Democracy Project poured $9.3 million into ads in that primary, per AdImpact, accounting for nearly half of the spending in the race. Sidney Clark, a Democratic candidate for state representative currently serving in local government, said he supported Bell in 2024 but was voting for Bush this cycle because Bell, in his view, has “been paid for.” “There are people out there who are using their money and financial influence to buy candidates, and I think that’s the wrong direction for our country,” Clark said after voting at a St. Louis polling place. Airest Wilson, another Democratic voter, told NBC News that candidates who take corporate money cross a red line for him — even if they are otherwise aligned with his political views. “They don’t get that money for free,” he said. “You got to represent their interests. You can’t represent the constituents freely.” “Cori, it took a lot of courage, but she rejected dark money. So that’s why I support Cori,” Wilson added. This year, Bush ran two TV ads in the primary, each touching on multiple issues. But both linked Bell to AIPAC and cast him as more interested in sending money to Israel than Missourians, including those suffering from the aftermath of last year’s tornado. Bell presented himself as a fighter against President Donald Trump, saying of Bush in one of his ads: “She fights Kamala Harris, Joe Biden, and other Democrats.” Bush said Tuesday that if she were to lose, it would not be a setback for the progressive movement. “If there is a loss, then that just means that there is more work for us to do,” she said. Asked if she could see herself voting for Bell if he wins the primary, Bush told NBC News, “See myself voting for a Republican? Oh, I don’t think that’s on the ballot for me.”
news.author: Brennan Leach,Sahil Kapur

news.title: Trump-backed Ty Masterson wins Republican nomination for Kansas governor
news.text: State Senate President Ty Masterson has won the Republican nomination in Kansas’ race for governor, NBC News projects, riding an endorsement from President Donald Trump to the general election in a state that is arguably the party’s best gubernatorial pickup opportunity. Masterson emerged from a primary field that included Secretary of State Scott Schwab, Insurance Commissioner Vicki Schmidt, businessman Philip Sarnecki and several others. He will face the winner of the Democratic gubernatorial primary, which includes state Sens. Cindy Holscher and Ethan Corson. Holscher has run a progressive, anti-establishment campaign, while Corson has leaned heavily on his support from term-limited Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly. Masterson and his allies were outspent on the airwaves by his GOP opponents, but his support from the president put him over the top. Trump won Kansas by double digits in each of the last three presidential elections. In a tele-rally last week, Trump lauded Masterson as a “fighter,” a “winner” and as someone who has “done a fantastic job — throughout life, actually.” “We love each other, we love that state,” Trump said. Kansas, where registered Republicans outnumber registered Democrats nearly 2 to 1, represents the GOP’s best opportunity to pick up a gubernatorial seat this fall.
news.author: Adam Edelman

news.title: Armed man detained at Trump golf course ahead of presidential visit
news.text:
An armed man was arrested after allegedly conducting suspicious surveillance at Donald Trump’s golf course in California ahead of the US president’s visit, police said.

Trump, who has survived several assassination attempts, is set to attend a Republican National Committee dinner at Trump National Golf Club in Rancho Palos Verdes on Tuesday evening.

According to the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department, deputies detained a “suspicious individual” on Sunday after he was seen taking photographs and videos on the property and appeared to be “monitoring security-planning activities.”

The man, identified as Jeanine John Teale, had a 16-round magazine loaded with hollow-point ammunition in his pocket. A loaded pistol and another magazine were found in a vehicle parked near the golf course.

Deputies obtained a warrant to search Teale’s home in Downey, where they found additional firearms, including an illegally modified AR-platform rifle, as well as body armor and two radios. The department said “multiple notebooks containing concerning statements” were also discovered at the residence.

Teale was arrested on weapons charges, the department said, adding that the ongoing investigation could result in further charges.

news.title: No one's talking about the other nomination battle Trump's losing
news.text:
President Donald Trump has fired much of the military’s top personnel and replaced them with loyalists, as well as engaged in controversial practices like encouraging personnel to receive testosterone supplements.

Joni Ernst and other Republican senators, according to U.S. officials and congressional sources,” reported The Wall Street Journal's Lara Seligman on Tuesday. “Hegseth has been pushing to nominate Gen. Christopher LaNeve, who has served as acting Army chief of staff since Hegseth in April fired the former Army top officer, retired Gen. Randy George, according to U.S. officials. But without unanimous Republican support, a LaNeve nomination won’t advance out of the Senate Armed Services Committee.”

Seligman added, “The administration was poised in May to put forward LaNeve for the role, but has held off because the committee chairman, Sen. Roger Wicker (R., Miss.), communicated that he didn’t have the votes to secure approval for LaNeve’s nomination, according to U.S. officials and congressional sources. LaNeve, who commanded the 82nd Airborne Division, has faced criticism from lawmakers and experts who note he has been a four-star general for only six months. Most chiefs serve at least 18 months in a four-star role before assuming the top position.”

Like many of the military personnel preferred by Trump, LaNeve has benefited from his perceived political support for the Republican leader.

“LaNeve’s reputation for discipline and a chance encounter with President Trump vaulted him into a senior position at the Pentagon last year,” Seligman wrote. “While commanding the Eighth Army in South Korea in January 2025, LaNeve appeared in a video call for an inaugural ball. ‘Welcome back, Mr. President,’ said the square-jawed general, reciting a script that had been vetted before the event, WSJ reported.”

Seligman added, “Trump appeared impressed. ‘Is this man central casting, or what?’ he asked the ballroom’s crowd.”

Trump’s management of the Defense Department has drawn considerable criticism for being more motivated by politics than merit. In July Margaret Donovan, a lawyer and Army JAG veteran, broke down the flaws of the Pentagon under Trump by analyzing how they got America into a war with Iran.

“You know, you get somebody like Secretary Hegseth in charge of the Department of Defense, and that's what you get,” Donovan told The Bulwark’s William Kristol on Thursday, describing how Trump got roughly 120 Iranian schoolgirls killed in a botched air strike.

“You get this harebrained operation, and the very first strike, something that, nearly every former military lawyer, probably current military lawyers, if they could speak freely would consider a war crime, or otherwise unauthorized under the law of armed conflict,” Donovan continued. “You have that, and lest you thought that was a fluke, that sort of rushing into an operation ill-prepared and not fully thought out in terms of your legal basis. We have February 28th, and so that's the opening of the Iran War.”
